verses.text: Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham's time. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar.
The LORD appeared to Isaac and said, "Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you.
Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands, and through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws."
So Isaac settled in Gerar.

But when the men of that place asked about his wife, he said, "She is my sister." For he was afraid to say, "She is my wife," since he thought to himself, "The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful."
When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, "So she is really your wife! How could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac replied, "Because I thought I might die on account of her."
"What is this you have done to us?" asked Abimelech. "One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."
So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death."
Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him,
and he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.
He owned so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines envied him.
So the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
Then Abimelech said to Isaac, "Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us."
So Isaac left that place and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.

Isaac reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham died. And he gave these wells the same names his father had given them.
Then Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen and said, "The water is ours!" So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him.
Then they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.
He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, "At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land."
From there Isaac went up to Beersheba,

and that night the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham."
So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and he pitched his tent there. His servants also dug a well there.
Later, Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
"Why have you come to me?" Isaac asked them. "You hated me and sent me away."
"We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you," they replied. "We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you. Let us make a covenant with you
that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you but have done only good to you, sending you on your way in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD."
So Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
And they got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
On that same day, Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug. "We have found water!" they told him.
So he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba.
When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Isaac’s sons, Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19 to 36:43)
context.audience: Israel, named for Jacob, learning how God kept His promise through a flawed and struggling family
context.setting: Another famine comes, and Isaac goes to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar (v.1). The LORD tells him, “Do not go down to Egypt,” and repeats to him the promise He gave Abraham: land, descendants “as numerous as the stars in the sky,” and blessing for all nations (vv.2-5). Like his father before him, Isaac says of his wife, “She is my sister” (v.7), until Abimelech sees him “caressing his wife Rebekah” and protects them both (vv.8-11). Isaac sows and reaps “a hundredfold” and grows so rich that the Philistines envy him and stop up Abraham’s wells (vv.12-15). Sent away, Isaac reopens his father’s wells and digs new ones; the herdsmen of Gerar fight over Esek and Sitnah, but at the third he says, “At last the LORD has made room for us” (vv.17-22). At Beersheba the LORD appears again: “Do not be afraid, for I am with you” (v.24). Abimelech comes asking for a treaty, “We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you” (v.28), and the same day Isaac’s servants find water (vv.26-33).
context.custom: In a land of little rain, a well was wealth and a claim to the land around it. Digging one took weeks of work, and stopping one up with dirt was an act of hostility. The well names tell the story: Esek means contention, Sitnah means opposition (from the same root as satan, adversary), and Rehoboth means wide places or room. Shibah (v.33) sounds like the Hebrew words for oath and for seven, and so explains the name Beersheba, well of the oath. Philistines are named here centuries before the Sea Peoples settled the coast about 1175 BC; the name may be used for the people of Gerar in the writer’s own day, or for an earlier group.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 27 tells how Rebekah and Jacob deceive the blind Isaac and take the blessing meant for Esau.
context.timelineBible: Isaac’s life is the quietest of the patriarchs’: he does not travel far, and most of what he does repeats his father, the famine, the wife called a sister, the wells and the treaty with Abimelech. God repeats His promise to him “for the sake of My servant Abraham” (v.24). Hebrews says Abraham “lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob” (Hebrews 11:9), heirs of a promise they did not yet hold.

translation.meaning: To be wide, to make room. Rehoboth, wide places, comes from this root. After two quarrels Isaac names the third well for the space God gave him.
To contend, to quarrel. The well Esek takes its name from this verb, used only here in the Bible.
An oath, often with a curse attached for whoever breaks it. Abimelech asks for a sworn treaty with the man God is blessing.

gospelParallels.note: Isaac and Jacob lived in tents as heirs of the same promise.
As far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.
Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?

otBackground.note: Abraham calls Sarah his sister at Gerar.
Abraham and Abimelech make a treaty at Beersheba.
You have relieved me in my distress.

overview.summary: Isaac stays in the land through a famine, repeats his father’s lie about his wife, grows rich, moves from well to well rather than fight, and receives God’s promise and a treaty at Beersheba.
overview.settingLine: Gerar and Beersheba, in the dry south.

history.t: The name is used of the people of Gerar long before the Philistine cities rose.
Drought sent herders toward Egypt; God tells Isaac to stay.

customs.t: A well marked a claim to the land and its pasture.
Each well’s name remembers what happened there.

archaeology.t: Often identified with Gerar, west of Beersheba.
A great well was found at the Israelite city.

overview.discussion: Isaac kept moving on rather than fighting for each well, and found room at last (v.22). Where am I fighting for a well that God may want me to leave behind?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: Stays, digs and receives the promise

historicalImage.caption: Isaac and Rebekah, from the frescoes of the Vatican Loggia designed by Raphael and painted by his workshop (1518-19). Abimelech learned they were husband and wife when he “looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah” (Genesis 26:8).

currentImage.caption: A deep well and stone trough at Tel Be’er Sheva. The well found there is usually dated to the Israelite town, centuries after Abraham, but it shows how much wells mattered in the Negev: “Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized” (Genesis 21:25).
